drink:DO Empordà reds.name: DO Empordà reds
drink:DO Empordà reds.teaser: Low bush vines bent by the tramuntana, in the most north-easterly wine zone in Spain
drink:DO Empordà reds.story: Drive north from Girona towards Figueres and the vineyards begin where the plain meets the Albera hills: squat, goblet-pruned bushes that the tramuntana keeps close to the ground and stingy with their crop. The DO was created by ministerial order on 19 May 1975 as Empordà–Costa Brava; in 2006 it dropped the coast from its name and took in the Baix Empordà. Its reds rest on two old grapes, Garnatxa negra, which the growers call lledoner, and Carinyena, with Cabernet, Merlot, Syrah and Ull de llebre planted since. Garnatxa alone fills about a third of the vineyard. Expect ripe dark fruit, warmth and a dry, herbal finish.
drink:DO Empordà reds.why: Order an Empordà red with grilled lamb or botifarra: the wine and the meat come from the same hills.
facts: Ripe black and red fruit, garrigue herbs, warmth; firmer and fresher when Carinyena leads the blend
DO Empordà; Garnatxa negra or lledoner, Carinyena or samsó; 'vinyes velles' marks old vines
Un negre de l'Empordà. Growers with their own larder card: the Empordà estates; around EUR 10–35 a bottle on a Girona list (seen Jun 2026)

drink:Garnatxa de l'Empordà.name: Garnatxa de l'Empordà
drink:Garnatxa de l'Empordà.teaser: Raisined in sun and wind, its ferment stopped with spirit: the amber glass that ends an Empordà lunch
drink:Garnatxa de l'Empordà.story: Every old farmhouse on the plain kept a cask of it for visitors and for the end of a feast. The grapes, chiefly the pale, pink-skinned Garnatxa roja with some blanca, hang until sun and tramuntana have half-dried them on the bunch. Their must is so rich that the makers add wine spirit partway through the ferment, stopping it while much of the sugar remains. Strengths run between about 14 and 20 per cent; one Perelada bottling stands at 15. Old ones age for years in tired barrels, going amber and tasting of fig, walnut and caramel. It shares a grape, but nothing else, with the dry reds.
drink:Garnatxa de l'Empordà.why: Pour it with a hard aged cheese or a plate of carquinyolis at the end of the meal, not with a fruit tart.
facts: Amber to mahogany; fig, raisin, walnut and toffee, more oxidative with age
DO Empordà, Garnatxa de l'Empordà, vi dolç natural; often a 50 cl bottle
Una copa de Garnatxa de l'Empordà. Names: Celler Cooperatiu d'Espolla, Perelada, Empordàlia, Espelt; around EUR 8–20 for a half bottle (seen Jun 2026)

drink:Vi novell.name: Vi novell
drink:Vi novell.teaser: This year's grapes in the glass by mid-November, opened the week the pigs were killed
drink:Vi novell.story: The farmers' saying fixes the calendar: per Sant Martí, mata el porc i enceta el vi. On or around 11 November, Saint Martin's day, the household killed its pig and broached the new barrel, and the Empordà still marks the date with a young wine. Vi novell is bottled only weeks after the harvest, with no ageing in wood, so it keeps the bright, grapey fruit of the vintage and, in some bottles, a faint prickle left by the ferment. It is a wine for the moment, drunk cool and quickly through November and December with roast chestnuts and the season's first sausages, not laid down.
drink:Vi novell.why: Ask for it from mid-November, and drink it before Christmas: it does not improve with keeping.
facts: Purple-red, light, juicy; fresh red berries and grape, little tannin, sometimes a slight spritz
Vi novell or vi nou, with the year of that autumn's harvest; DO Empordà
Un vi novell de l'Empordà; the Celler Cooperatiu d'Espolla bottles a well-known one. Around EUR 5–10 (seen Jun 2026)

drink:Vermut.name: Vermut de l'Empordà
drink:Vermut.teaser: Sunday at noon, a short glass of vermut on a terrace before the long lunch
drink:Vermut.story: In Girona the hour before Sunday lunch belongs to the vermut: a short tumbler, ice, a slice of orange, an olive on a stick, and a dish of crisps or anchovies alongside. Most of what is poured is the dark, sweet, bitter style made around Reus, but some Empordà cellars now build a vermouth on their own wine. The old guide names Celler Gerisena at Garriguella, which works with the native Garnatxa roja, and a two-year oak-aged bottling called Obreboques; Gerisena's Garnatxa roja wines are well documented, but we could not reconfirm the vermouth in October 2026. Arcaded terraces in the Barri Vell are the natural place to take it.
drink:Vermut.why: Take it at noon with something salty, then go straight on to lunch: that is the whole point of it.
facts: Mahogany; bitter herbs, orange peel, a sweet core; on garnatxa roja, more wine than syrup
Vermut negre (sweet red) or blanc; the maker's village tells you whether it is from the Empordà
Un vermut de la casa amb sifó, or ask whether there is one from the Empordà. Around EUR 10–18 a bottle (seen Jun 2026)

drink:Ratafia.name: Ratafia
drink:Ratafia.teaser: Green walnuts picked in early summer, steeped with herbs in spirit and poured dark after the coffee
drink:Ratafia.story: Ratafia is made in June and July, when the walnuts on the tree are still green enough to slice straight through. Families steep them in spirit with their own secret mix of herbs and spices and set the jars out in sun and night dew for about forty days. The protected version, Ratafia Catalana IGP, asks for at least three months of maceration and three more in wood, with lemon verbena, cinnamon, clove and nutmeg in the blend, bottled at 24 to 30 per cent. Santa Coloma de Farners, south of Girona, holds its Festa de la Ratafia on the second weekend of November and a home-makers' contest begun in 1982.
drink:Ratafia.why: Ask whether the house has its own: a plain unlabelled bottle from a village is often the best pour in the room.
facts: Dark brown; green walnut, clove, cinnamon and herbs; sweet, then dry and slightly bitter

Una ratafia, cool. Festa de la Ratafia, Santa Coloma de Farners: listed for 13–15 November 2026 (Oct 2026). To make your own, La Sobirana's workshop has its card under Craft; around EUR 10–20 a bottle (seen Jun 2026)

drink:Cremat.name: Cremat
drink:Cremat.teaser: A clay dish of rum, sugar and coffee set alight, stirred in its own blue flame and ladled hot
drink:Cremat.story: Cremat means burnt, and that is the method. A wide earthenware cassola takes dark rum, sugar, a stick of cinnamon, lemon peel and a few coffee beans. A match goes in, and for several minutes someone lifts the burning rum on a ladle and lets it fall back, so the sugar caramelises and much of the alcohol flames off. Strong coffee is poured over to put the fire out, and the result goes into small cups, scalding, sweet and smoky. The rum is a souvenir of the nineteenth-century sailing trade between this coast and Cuba, the same voyages that brought home the havanera songs.
drink:Cremat.why: Have it lit at the table on a cool night by the sea; watching the flame is half of the drink.
facts: Hot; burnt sugar, coffee, cinnamon, lemon, with the rum softened by the burning
Not bottled: made to order in the bowl, mostly on the coast in summer
Un cremat per a la taula. The songs sung over it have their own card under Listening; Calella de Palafrugell, its home ground, is in the Costa Brava guide

listening:No hi-fi bar in Girona.name: No hi-fi bar in Girona
listening:No hi-fi bar in Girona.teaser: We searched for a vinyl or hi-fi listening bar in Girona and found nowhere to send you
listening:No hi-fi bar in Girona.story: Listening bars, small rooms built around a serious sound system and a wall of records, where the point is to sit and hear an album properly, have reached many large European cities. Girona does not have one yet. In October 2026 we searched in English, Catalan and Spanish through press, venue listings and Time Out Girona, and found wine bars, cocktail bars, clubs and a jazz cellar, but no room run for listening. The nearest things are a 50-seat jazz club where the audience actually keeps quiet, and a café that sells records and plays them while you eat.
listening:No hi-fi bar in Girona.why: For music you sit still for, book the jazz club on a weekend night instead.
facts: Nothing to visit: no hi-fi or vinyl listening bar found in Girona (searched Oct 2026)

listening:Sunset Jazz Club, for the reco.name: Sunset Jazz Club, for the record
listening:Sunset Jazz Club, for the reco.teaser: The one room in Girona where a crowd sits still for the music: a stone cellar of about fifty seats
listening:Sunset Jazz Club, for the reco.story: If you want to listen rather than talk over a soundtrack, this is the address. The vaulted cellar is small, and the members who keep it going expect silence during a set. The club turns 25 on 3 November 2026, and Ara reported an anniversary programme for this autumn. Go on a Saturday for the late set and keep your phone away.
listening:Sunset Jazz Club, for the reco.why: Come for the second set on a weekend night, when the room is fullest and quietest.
facts: A glass at the bar through the set; there is no kitchen

listening:La Santa Espina.name: La Santa Espina
listening:La Santa Espina.teaser: A sardana tune so loaded with meaning that two dictatorships forbade it
listening:La Santa Espina.story: Enric Morera wrote the music and Àngel Guimerà the words, and the piece was first heard in 1907. Its sardana became the most charged in the repertoire: the melody of a circle dance that reads, to many Catalans, as a national hymn. Both the Primo de Rivera regime and Franco's barred it, which only fixed it deeper in memory. Today a cobla usually saves it for a significant moment, and you will notice the change in the square: hands join a little more firmly, the older dancers are first into the ring, and some people sing along under their breath.
listening:La Santa Espina.why: If you hear the opening bars at an audició, watch the oldest dancers rather than the band.
facts: Sardana audicions in Girona's squares and at the Fires de Sant Narcís (23 Oct–1 Nov 2026), which have their own calendar card; the cobla picks the programme, so it is never guaranteed

listening:Cobla La Principal de la Bisba.name: Cobla La Principal de la Bisbal
listening:Cobla La Principal de la Bisba.teaser: Eleven players, a reedy tenora and a tiny flabiol: the Empordà band that plays the sardana for Catalonia
listening:Cobla La Principal de la Bisba.story: A cobla is the eleven-piece band of the sardana: a three-holed flabiol played with one hand while the other taps a little drum, the double-reeded tible and tenora, brass, and a double bass. The tenora's nasal, almost oboe-like cry is the sound to listen for. La Principal de la Bisbal comes from the pottery town of La Bisbal d'Empordà and holds the title of official cobla of the Generalitat, restored in 1978. Girona's Auditori has booked it for its Sant Narcís concert; in 2025 it played there on 29 October under Francesc Cassú. On a square, its tunes are what set the circle dancers counting steps.
listening:Cobla La Principal de la Bisba.why: Hear it once live: on a recording the tenora sounds quaint, in a stone square it cuts like a trumpet.
facts: Its next date we found is the Festa Petita at Vidreres, 13–15 November 2026 (Oct 2026); a Fires de Sant Narcís 2026 concert was not confirmed when we checked

listening:Nits de Clàssica.name: Nits de Clàssica
listening:Nits de Clàssica.teaser: Summer evenings when the Auditori moved its soloists into the cathedral, the cloister and a Romanesque nave
listening:Nits de Clàssica.story: For years Girona's summer classical cycle, run by the Auditori, took chamber players out of the concert hall and into the old town's stone: the Cathedral, its cloister and the church of Sant Pere de Galligants. A single violin in the cathedral's enormous nave rings on for seconds after the bow stops; in the cloister the swifts sometimes join in. The 2019 edition, the eighth, ran 26 June to 30 July with sixteen concerts. We could not find a 2026 edition, and the Auditori's published plans for 2026–27 do not mention one, so treat this as a cycle to check for, not to count on.
listening:Nits de Clàssica.why: If a summer concert is announced in the cathedral or cloister, book it: the acoustics are the point.
facts: Girona Cathedral, its cloister and Sant Pere de Galligants, each with its own card under Culture
Late June to July in past editions (2019: 26 Jun–30 Jul); no 2026 edition found (Oct 2026)
Evening concerts, as the name says

listening:El meu avi and the havaneres.name: El meu avi and the havaneres
listening:El meu avi and the havaneres.teaser: A 1968 song about a grandfather's ship lost off Cuba, and the beach night it used to close
listening:El meu avi and the havaneres.story: Havaneres are slow songs in the swaying habanera rhythm that Catalan crews carried home from the nineteenth-century Cuba trade, sung to guitar and accordion over a burning cremat. The best known, El meu avi, dates from 1968 and tells of an old sailor and his ship, the Català, lost in the war of 1898. For decades the whole beach at Calella de Palafrugell sang it together to end the July Cantada. In 2025 it was taken off the close after a 3Cat documentary about its late author; for 2026 the new director put it back into the communal singing, and then the night itself was called off.
listening:El meu avi and the havaneres.why: Learn the chorus before you go: at a cantada the crowd sings, it does not just listen.
facts: The Cantada d'Havaneres at Calella de Palafrugell, traditionally the first Saturday of July; the 2026 night (4 July) was cancelled for a nearby wildfire. Calella has its own card in the Costa Brava guide
Its place at the Cantada: dropped from the finale in 2025, restored to the shared singing for 2026; the author's family called the 2025 decision censorship, noting his acquittals in the 1980s

around:Besalú.name: Besalú
around:Besalú.teaser: A crooked stone bridge with a gate tower midway, and a medieval ritual bath under the old Jewish streets
around:Besalú.story: You see Besalú before you reach it: the Pont Vell, a long Romanesque bridge that bends at an angle over the Fluvià, with a fortified gateway standing halfway across. Walk through it into lanes of brown stone and you are in one of the best-kept medieval towns in Catalonia. Near the river, in what was the Jewish quarter, the town uncovered in 1964 a twelfth-century mikveh, a barrel-vaulted ritual bath fed by groundwater and the first found in Spain. You go down to it only with the short guided visit run by the tourist office, which also shows the outline of the synagogue above. Come early, ahead of the coaches.
around:Besalú.why: Take the guided visit down into the mikveh: its cold, silent vault is the reason to stop.
facts: About 35 km north-west of Girona by road, via Banyoles; roughly 40 minutes
A half day, or a stop on the way to Olot

The Pont Vell and the mikveh: guided visit from the tourist office, C/ Pont 1, EUR 2.25, daily 13:30 and 17:30 except Tuesday and Thursday, about 30 minutes (besalu.cat, undated page, seen Oct 2026; confirm)

around:Banyoles and its lake.name: Banyoles and its lake
around:Banyoles and its lake.teaser: Catalonia's largest natural lake, flat calm and fringed with reeds, where the 1992 Olympic rowers raced
around:Banyoles and its lake.story: Twenty minutes north of Girona the land opens onto a long sheet of still water: the Estany de Banyoles, fed from below by springs and the largest natural lake in Catalonia. In 1992 it hosted the Olympic rowing regatta, and crews still train on it at dawn. A level path circles the whole shore under plane trees and through reed beds, past wooden fishing huts and the small ponds called estanyols, with the town's arcaded square a short walk from the southern end. The lake is a protected natural area, part of Natura 2000. October brings mist on the water first thing and very few visitors.
around:Banyoles and its lake.why: Walk the full loop in the morning, when the water is still and the rowers are out.
facts: About 20 minutes by car north of Girona on the C-66
Half a day: about two hours for the loop, plus the old town
The signposted Volta a l'Estany, a flat circuit of about 7 to 8 km (sources differ, Oct 2026); and the 2 km wetland path by the Puda and Estunes

around:Olot and the Garrotxa volcanoes.name: Olot and the Garrotxa volcanoes
around:Olot and the Garrotxa volcanoes.teaser: Forty-odd sleeping cones under grass and oak, and a beech wood that grew on a lava flow
around:Olot and the Garrotxa volcanoes.story: Beyond Besalú the hills begin to look suspiciously round. Around Olot about forty extinct volcanoes stand under woods and meadows, protected since 1985 as the Zona Volcànica de la Garrotxa natural park. Santa Margarida holds a near-perfect crater with a little Romanesque chapel alone on the grass at the bottom. Croscat, the youngest cone on the peninsula, was quarried for its red gravel until the cut exposed its inner layers like a sliced cake. The Fageda d'en Jordà beech wood grows on a flat lava flow at about 550 metres and turns copper in late October. The beans of nearby Santa Pau have their own card in the Larder.
around:Olot and the Garrotxa volcanoes.why: Walk the Fageda d'en Jordà now, in late October, while the beech leaves are turning.
facts: By car via Banyoles and Besalú, under an hour from Girona; Besalú has its own card
A full day for a crater, the beech wood and lunch
Santa Margarida's crater chapel, the Croscat cross-section and the Fageda d'en Jordà

around:The Costa Brava.name: The Costa Brava
around:The Costa Brava.teaser: Pine-backed coves, fishing ports and cliff paths within an hour of the Barri Vell: it has its own guide
around:The Costa Brava.story: From Girona the sea is closer than most visitors think. Head east across the Baix Empordà and within the hour you reach Calella de Palafrugell, with its whitewashed arches over a beach of fishing boats, and the cliff path that runs to Llafranc. Palamós auctions its red prawns on the quay each afternoon; L'Escala salts anchovies to a recipe it has kept for centuries. None of it is retold here: the coast has its own Littoralicious guide, with its walks, markets and tables, and it is the right companion for any crew moving between Girona and the boat.
around:The Costa Brava.why: Make it a full day by the water, and use the Costa Brava guide to choose which stretch.
facts: By car about 45 minutes to an hour; Moventis Sarfa buses run Girona to Palafrugell, roughly hourly, about 1 hour to 1 h 20 (aggregators, Oct 2026; check moventis.es), then a short hop to Calella
Calella's Port Bo, the camí de ronda to Llafranc, the Palamós fish auction; each has a card in the Costa Brava guide at /terroir/Costa-Brava-Catalunya/

around:Cadaqués.name: Cadaqués
around:Cadaqués.teaser: A white fishing town at the end of a twisting road over Cap de Creus: it has its own guide
around:Cadaqués.story: Cadaqués sits at the far end of the Empordà, where the Pyrenees run into the sea at Cap de Creus: a white town around a bay of slate and fishing boats, cut off for centuries by the mountain behind it. Dalí spent his summers at Portlligat, a short walk over the hill. Getting there is half the story. After Figueres and Roses the last stretch climbs into bare, wind-scoured rock and twists down to the water. Everything worth doing there is covered in the sister guide, from the cape's walks to the Dalí house; this card only tells you how far it is.
around:Cadaqués.why: Go for a full day and leave early: the last road is slow and parking in town is tight.
facts: About 75 km by car via Figueres and Roses, about 1 h to 1 h 15; the final road from Roses is narrow and full of bends. Buses take about 1 h 45
The old town above the bay, Portlligat and Cap de Creus; each has a card in the Cadaqués guide at /terroir/Cadaques-CapdeCreus/
